notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 72, each followed by its source. A few limits first. I couldn't reach netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org or the Orthodox sites, so the "modern scholarship" points come from older commentators who report critical views. I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this psalm, so there's no section on them. Gill's full commentary didn't load, so I only have a few of his notes. I sorted the Enduring Word notes under "Pentecostal and charismatic" because that's how your site list groups the site.

**Introduction and title (v. 1 heading)**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik suggests Solomon may have put together Book Two of the Psalms and written this psalm to close it. He sees its focus as the Messiah, the Son of David, more than Solomon or David. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/
- Matthew Henry says it must be about Christ's kingdom, because "there are many passages in it which cannot be applied to the reign of Solomon." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_072.cfm
- **Reformed (who wrote it):** Calvin reads it as David praying "in the name of the whole Church, for the continual prosperity of the kingdom which was promised him". Because verse 20 calls it the last of David's prayers, he thinks David wrote it rather than Solomon. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_3/psalm_72.htm
- **Baptist (who wrote it):** Spurgeon's notes say the old commentators assigned the psalm to David because they misread verse 20. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps072.cfm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Things in the psalm don't fit the earthly Solomon, so the name stands for Christ. "Solomon" means "peacemaker," and Christ reconciles enemies to God. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801072.htm
- **Modern views (as Ellicott reports them):** Ewald suggested Josiah as the king, and Hitzig and Reuss a foreign ruler, Ptolemy Philadelphus. Ellicott himself finds the messianic reading fits best. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-72.html

**v. 1**
- Guzik: this is the same heart behind Solomon's request for wisdom in 1 Kings 3:5–9. Kidner, quoted there, notes that the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) adds "Messiah" to "the king." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/
- Pulpit Commentary: Solomon calls himself both "king" and "king's son" to appeal to respect for a hereditary throne. He is asking for a spirit of judgment so his decisions would be as righteous as God's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/72.htm
- Spurgeon: Israel's kings were only deputies of the greater King, so the prayer asks for divine right and divine wisdom. Christ has all judgment committed to him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps072.cfm
- Gill: the King is Christ, which he says was also the view of the old Jewish synagogue. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-72.html
- Catholic (Augustine): links the verse to John 5:22, where the Father gives all judgment to the Son. The King is also the King's Son because the Father is King too. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801072.htm

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: the words run "judgments, righteousness, righteousness, judgment," a mirrored parallel. They mean the practical skill of judging in government, and Solomon's prayer at Gibeon (1 Kings 3:9) is the best comment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/72.htm
- Catholic (Augustine): "your people" and "your poor" are the same group, which shows God's people should be poor in the sense of humble (Matthew 5:3). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801072.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik, drawing on Spurgeon: there are several ideas of what the "mountains" mean. Messengers relaying news from hilltops, fertile mountain soil, or safety from robbers in mountain passes. Maclaren says they are simply the land's most prominent features. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/
- Ellicott: the verb can mean "bear fruit," so the mountains "bring forth" peace in righteousness. Isaiah 32:17 calls peace the fruit of righteousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/72.htm
- Geneva Bible notes: when justice reigns, even the most barren places will be enriched. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gsb/psalms/72.htm
- Catholic (Augustine): the mountains are leading saints of the Church and the hills are those who follow them. Leaders must work for peace and not cause schisms. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801072.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: the king will see justice done for the poor, rescue the vulnerable, and protect the nation from enemies outside and corruption inside. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/
- Pulpit: the poor are the king's special concern, though not his only one. Israel's unjust rulers neglected exactly this (Jeremiah 5:28). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/72.htm
- Geneva Bible notes: this shows why kings are given the sword, to defend the innocent and hold down the wicked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gsb/psalms/72.htm
- Catholic (Augustine): the "oppressor" or false accuser is best seen as the devil. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801072.htm

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: "as long as the sun and moon" means for all time. He says the question of whether God or the king is the one feared "must remain unanswered." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-72.html
- Pulpit: the one feared is God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/72-5.htm
- Matthew Henry: Solomon's temple worship didn't last, so this points to Christ's kingdom. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_072.cfm
- Calvin: the sun-and-moon phrases are Hebrew idioms for how eternal the Messiah's kingdom is. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/72.htm
- Catholic (Augustine): the Church, Christ's body on earth, will last as long as the sun keeps rising. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801072.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: good rule refreshes like rain, as in David's last words (2 Samuel 23:4). The Hebrew word means "a shearing," and the Greek and Latin Bibles and the Prayer Book take it as "fleece." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/72.htm
- Matthew Henry: Christ comes down by his Spirit like rain on grass that is left growing after mowing, so it can spring up again. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/72.htm
- Catholic (Augustine): reading "fleece," he says Gideon's sign (Judges 6) finds its fulfilment in Christ. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801072.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik: righteousness and peace together recall Melchizedek, king of righteousness and king of peace (Hebrews 7). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/
- Gill: this is peace with God through Christ's blood, with more peace among the saints in the "latter day." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/72-7.htm
- Constable: the king is the subject of verses 6–7. A just king blesses his people as rain blesses the land. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/72-7.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik: this is the turning point, where Solomon looks past his own reign to a greater Son of David. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/
- Pulpit: no particular seas are meant. Messiah's rule reaches "from shore to shore." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/72-8.htm
- Ellicott: the River is certainly the Euphrates. He weighs whether exact borders are meant (Exodus 23:31) or just a vast empire, and leans toward the poetic reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/72.htm
- Geneva Bible notes: Christ's kingdom will be large and universal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gsb/psalms/72.htm
- The Seedbed article (in the Wesleyan group) says "no earthly king, even Solomon at the peak of his power, could fulfill the ideals of this psalm." https://seedbed.com/the-righteous-king-psalm-72/

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: the word probably means desert nomads, though the Greek and other ancient versions read "Ethiopians." "Lick the dust" refers to the Eastern custom of lying face-down before a ruler. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/72.htm
- Guzik connects "lick the dust" to the curse on the serpent in Genesis 3:14–15. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: "the isles" means Mediterranean coasts, Sheba stands for Arabia, and Seba stands for Africa. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-72.html
- Clarke: the gift brought was a friendly offering, not tribute. The Queen of Sheba's gifts weren't tribute either, since Solomon had no rule over her land. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/72-10.html
- Gill: this will be fulfilled when the kings of the earth bring their glory into the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:24). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/72-10.html
- **Lutheran (Epiphany):** 1517.org ties these verses to the Magi at Epiphany and calls Jesus "the new and better Solomon." https://www.1517.org/articles/why-not-diapers-and-casseroles-instead-of-gold-frankincense-and-myrrh
- **Wesleyan:** Seedbed also links the verse to the Magi's gifts. https://seedbed.com/the-righteous-king-psalm-72/
- Coffman quotes a writer who says the Church rightly made this the chief psalm of Epiphany. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-72.html

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: better translated as a wish, "Let all kings…" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/72.htm
- Smith links the verse to Philippians 2:10–11, every knee bowing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/72-10.html
- Catholic (Augustine): the "gifts" kings bring may be people that kings lead into the Church. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801072.htm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: "for" gives the reason for the king's wide rule, which is his justice to the weak. The verse almost repeats Job 29:12. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/72.htm
- Calvin: the kingdom described here will not be tyrannical or cruel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/72-12.html

**v. 13**
- Guzik: the KJV reads "save the souls of the needy," which goes beyond social work to saving souls. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/

**v. 14**
- Guzik quotes Maclaren: the king acts as Goel, the kinsman-redeemer. He also stresses how valuable human life is to him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/
- Ellicott: the parallel lines show the meaning. The king values his people's lives, so he protects them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/72.htm

**v. 15 (a real split over who "he" is)**
- **Traditional reading:** Pulpit says the Messiah lives on. His people pray for him the way Christians pray "Thy kingdom come" (citing Hengstenberg). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/72.htm
- Guzik agrees and takes "he shall live" as both a wish and a statement about the King. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/
- **Other reading:** Ellicott says the one who "lives" is the rescued poor person from verse 14, who then gives to and blesses the king. He calls the Prayer Book's "prayer shall be made to him" "quite inadmissible." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/72.htm
- Matthew Henry's line, quoted on Bible Hub, takes it as prayer made "through him, or for his sake," in his name. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/72-17.htm

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: "a handful" is better translated "abundance." Grain waves on the mountaintops like the cedars of Lebanon. He suggests the text may originally have read "let cities spring up like grass." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-72.html
- Geneva Bible notes: under such a king there will be plenty of fruit and many more people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gsb/psalms/72.htm
- Guzik quotes a writer who says the Israelites saw the moral world and nature as one whole. A righteous community also prospers in field and flock. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/

**v. 17**
- Guzik: this fulfils the promise to David (2 Samuel 7) and to Abraham (Genesis 12:3). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/
- Barnes: the Hebrew verb means "to sprout," like a tree that never dies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/72-17.htm
- Benson: this hardly fits Solomon, who spoiled his reign with luxury and turning from God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/72-17.htm
- Bible Hub's study page links "all nations blessed" to Galatians 3:16. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/72.htm

**vv. 18–19**
- Pulpit: this doxology marks the end of Book Two of the Psalms. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-72.html
- Guzik: Solomon is moved to praise by the vision of the Messiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/
- Matthew Henry: we are taught to bless God in Christ and to pray for the gospel to spread. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/72.htm

**v. 20**
- Spurgeon's notes list several readings and favour "here they are perfected," meaning David's prayers reach their goal. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps072.cfm
- Gill: David's prayers will only be fully answered when everything in this psalm is fulfilled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/72-20.htm
- Guzik: David is called simply "son of Jesse," taking the lower place before the greater Son. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-72.cfm

**Where views on the kingdom differ (whole psalm)**
- **Personal, future rule (Enduring Word, Constable):** Guzik says the psalm describes the King's personal rule, "not ruling through an institution such as the Church." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-72/ Constable (Dallas Seminary) says it looks ahead to Christ ruling on earth in the future. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/72-7.html
- **Spread of Christ's kingdom now:** Matthew Henry and Gill see it fulfilled as Christ's kingdom spreads through history, with Christianity lasting to the end of time. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_072.cfm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** reads the psalm in terms of the Church, Christ's body on earth. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801072.htm
